::: {.lede}
You are reading a computational psychiatry paper. There is a model name, a few
Greek letters, and a sentence saying some parameter was higher in the patient
group. This note is about what that sentence claims, and more usefully, what it
does not.
:::

No equations. The aim is not to let you build the model but to know where to
look when someone else's model produces a claim. For the mathematics and working
code, [Perception, Beliefs, and the Hierarchical Gaussian
Filter](https://metaduck.com/computational-psychiatry-afterburn-hierarchical-gaussian-filters/)
builds it step by step with `pyhgf`.

## The problem it solves {.k-head}

Suppose you watch a patient learn something. Say they are working out which of
two boxes pays out more often. What you have is a sequence of trial-by-trial
answers: A on this one, B on the next, then A again.

What can you read off that sequence? At the simplest you count how often they
were right. That number says nothing about how the learning happened. Two
patients can score identically having taken completely different routes: one
revised on every new piece of evidence, the other held out and then switched all
at once.

The Hierarchical Gaussian Filter assumes there is a person behind the sequence
and describes how that person learns with a handful of numbers. What it models
is not the behaviour but the process producing it.

## What the hierarchy means {.k-head}

The "hierarchical" in the name refers to layers of uncertainty stacked on one
another.

The bottom layer is the current state: is this box paying out right now. Above
it sits the tendency: how often does this box pay out in general. The top layer
is how changeable the world is, meaning how often those rules shift.

That third layer is the model's real idea and the one with the most clinical
purchase. How fast you ought to learn depends on how much the world actually
changes. If the rules shift often, revising quickly is sensible. If they are
fixed, the same speed has you chasing noise.

People make this adjustment constantly and the model puts a number on it.
Someone who takes the world to be more volatile than it is treats a single event
as too informative. Someone who takes the opposite view is slow to notice a real
change.

## What the parameters say clinically {.k-head}

The number reported most often is the learning rate, and the HGF's difference is
that the rate is not fixed. In classical learning models a person has one
learning speed and it stays the same from trial to trial. Here it is recomputed
on every trial, and it depends on how certain the person is at that moment and
how volatile they take the world to be. Learning speeds up after a surprise and
slows inside a familiar pattern.

The quantity governing this is precision. It has nothing to do with precision in
the everyday sense; it measures how narrow a belief is. A narrow belief leaves
little room for new evidence, a wide one leaves a lot. That is the clinically
interesting part: the source of a symptom may not be the evidence but the weight
given to it.

The engine is prediction error, the gap between what happened and what was
expected. The raw gap is not what gets used; the precision-weighted version is.
A surprise of the same size produces a different result depending on how certain
the person was.

There is also response noise, which absorbs everything the model cannot explain.
People do not always act on their beliefs; they get distracted, press the wrong
key, waver. Having this parameter matters, because without it disorderly
behaviour would look like a strange style of learning.

The appeal of these numbers is obvious. Each resembles a mechanism and attaches
easily to a clinical story. The two sections below are largely against that
ease.

## Why model comparison is not optional {.k-head}

A model was fitted and numbers came out. For those numbers to mean anything you
first have to know whether this model generated the data, or whether some other
model would have generated it just as well.

Goodness of fit does not answer that. A flexible enough model fits any data
well, and a good fit may be showing you flexibility rather than truth.

So fitting one model and reporting its numbers is not enough. Several candidate
models are built, all fitted to the same data, and compared on how well each
explains it. Because the comparison separately penalises complex models, adding
parameters to improve the fit does not count as winning.

If a paper has no model comparison, the parameters it reports do not point at a
mechanism. They are what you get when you summarise the data through that
particular model. The difference is not a small one.

## When to trust a finding {.k-head}

When a model fits, it produces a number for every parameter. That a number was
produced does not mean the data carried information about that parameter. In
some models two parameters move together: raise one and lower the other and the
model behaves identically. Their combination can then be read off the data but
neither can be read alone. The estimator still returns a number, because it has
to. That number reflects setup choices more than it reflects data.

The technical name for this is identifiability. It is among the first things to
ask about a computational finding.

The test is parameter recovery. You generate synthetic data from known values,
run the same pipeline over it, and check whether the values you put in come back
out. If they do not, the parameter cannot be measured with that design, and
there is no way to discover this from real data. I ran this on my own pipeline
before collecting anything, and I think the order matters: leave it until
afterwards and, when the result is bad, you are holding a number you could
publish, which makes it harder to drop.

Finally, parameter names. Calling a parameter "belief instability" or "learning
flexibility" does not establish that it measures that. The name is the
interpretation of whoever built the model. The same number can be attached to a
completely different mechanism under another reading, and choosing between the
two takes more than the model.

## In short {.k-head}

The HGF's clinical value is that it treats learning speed as an adjustment
tracking how volatile a person takes the world to be, rather than as a fixed
trait.

But not every number it produces is a mechanism. The estimator returns a number
under any conditions; what shows the number measures something is not the number
itself but the model comparison and the recovery behind it. Without both, what
you are holding is a summary statistic rather than a claim about mechanism. And
if the parameter's name is confident enough, that summary statistic gets read as
a mechanism.
